paragraphs.text: **1. A child needs a placement the district cannot give itself.** A private school or a collaborative, often with a van to get there. The law has Lunenburg pay from the day it starts. For a child who moves in already in a private school, the former town pays the rest of that year, so most move-ins are a next-year cost (Move-ins).

**2. It often lands late, and it is big for one line.** 92% of orders placed after September came March to June. A special education line spent past its vote in 13 of 17 years: $116,811 in a median recent bad year, $223,774 at worst.

**3. Chapter 70 and IDEA do not move.** Chapter 70, $9,229,410 in FY2026, is 35% of the school budget, set by a formula before the year begins; it assumes 1% of children are placed out of district, whatever the real number. IDEA, $437,380 allocated for FY2027, is a fixed federal grant.

**4. The circuit breaker repays part, a year later, and the vote already spent it.** The state repays a share of the costliest children: $579,142 for 9 children in FY2026, 46.1% of their costs. But the tuition vote is set after subtracting the repayment expected, $480,204 for FY2026.

**5. So what is left lands on the town budget.** A new placement is paid in full until the repayment catches up; a repayment smaller than expected leaves a gap the same size. Either is met from slack in other lines, or from a reserve, spent only by a vote of both boards.
